questions.question_text: At which OSI model layer does the Router primarily operate?
questions.option_b: Network Layer (Layer 3)
questions.explanation: Routers operate at the Network Layer (Layer 3) examining IP packet headers to make routing and forwarding decisions.

questions.question_text: At which layer of the OSI model does a network switch primarily operate?
questions.option_b: Layer 2 (Data Link)
questions.explanation: Standard Layer 2 Ethernet switches forward frames based on destination MAC addresses at the Data Link layer.

questions.question_text: DNS purpose?
questions.option_b: Translate domains to IPs
questions.explanation: DNS=Domain Name System

questions.question_text: HTTP 404 means?
questions.option_b: Unauthorized
questions.explanation: 404=resource not found

questions.question_text: How many layers are in the OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) reference model?
questions.explanation: The OSI model consists of 7 layers: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, and Application.

questions.question_text: What does ARP stand for?
questions.option_b: Advanced Routing Protocol
questions.explanation: Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) resolves network layer IPv4 addresses to physical MAC addresses on a local subnet.

questions.question_text: What does MAC stand for in networking?
questions.option_b: Memory Allocation Control
questions.explanation: MAC (Media Access Control) address is a unique hardware identifier assigned to a network interface controller (NIC).

questions.question_text: What is the loopback IPv4 address typically assigned to localhost?
questions.explanation: 127.0.0.1 (part of the 127.0.0.0/8 block) is designated for the local loopback interface.

questions.question_text: What is the size of an IPv4 address?
questions.option_b: 32 bits
questions.explanation: An IPv4 address consists of 32 bits (4 octets), typically represented in dotted-decimal format (e.g., 192.168.1.1).

questions.question_text: What is the size of an IPv6 address?
questions.option_b: 64 bits
questions.explanation: An IPv6 address is 128 bits in length, represented as 8 groups of 4 hexadecimal digits.

questions.question_text: What is the standard port number for secure web browsing (HTTPS)?
questions.explanation: HTTPS communicates over port 443 by default, whereas unencrypted HTTP uses port 80.

questions.question_text: Which command is used to test reachability of a host on an IP network?
questions.option_b: traceroute
questions.explanation: The ping utility sends ICMP Echo Request messages to test the reachability and round-trip time to a remote host.

questions.question_text: Which protocol is used to assign dynamic IP addresses to devices on a network?
questions.option_b: DHCP
questions.explanation: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) automatically assigns IP addresses and network configuration to client devices.

questions.question_text: Which protocol translates human-friendly domain names (e.g., google.com) into IP addresses?
questions.option_b: DNS
questions.explanation: Domain Name System (DNS) maintains a distributed database mapping domain names to numerical IP addresses.

questions.question_text: Which transport layer protocol is connectionless and does not guarantee packet delivery?
questions.option_b: UDP
questions.explanation: UDP (User Datagram Protocol) provides a lightweight, connectionless datagram service without acknowledgments or retransmissions.

questions.question_text: How does Random Early Detection (RED) buffer management prevent global TCP synchronization?
questions.option_a: Discards all packets when buffer is 50% full
questions.option_b: Probabilistically drops incoming packets before the queue becomes full, causing individual TCP flows to back off at different times
questions.option_d: Allocates static queues per IP address
questions.explanation: By dropping packets probabilistically based on average queue length, RED avoids simultaneous timeouts across all TCP connections sharing a bottleneck link.

questions.question_text: How does the Nagle's algorithm optimize TCP transmission, and how does it interact with Delayed ACKs?
questions.option_a: Compresses IP headers; eliminates all ACK delays
questions.option_b: Buffers small outgoing packets until a full MSS is accumulated or previous ACK received; causes deadlocks/delays with Delayed ACKs
questions.option_c: Encapsulates TCP in UDP; bypasses flow control
questions.explanation: Nagle delays sending partial packets while waiting for outstanding ACKs, causing noticeable ~200ms latency spikes when the receiver uses Delayed ACKs.

questions.question_text: In BGP path selection, what is the FIRST tiebreaker evaluated among valid paths to the same prefix?
questions.option_b: Highest Weight (Cisco-specific) or Highest Local Preference (standard)
questions.explanation: BGP prefers the highest Local Preference (or highest proprietary Weight on Cisco routers) before inspecting AS-Path length.

questions.question_text: In Distance Vector routing, what technique sends a metric of 16 (infinity) back to the neighbor through which the route was learned?
questions.option_b: Counting to Infinity
questions.explanation: Poison Reverse actively advertises unreachable cost back to the source neighbor to immediately prevent 2-node routing loops.

questions.question_text: In IPv4 subnetting with a subnet mask of 255.255.255.224 (/27), how many usable host IP addresses are available in each subnet?
questions.explanation: 32 - 27 = 5 host bits. Total IPs = 2^5 = 32. Subtracting 2 for Network ID and Broadcast address yields 30 usable host IP addresses.

questions.question_text: In TCP Reno congestion control, what happens upon receiving 3 duplicate ACKs (Fast Retransmit)?
questions.option_a: Slow start threshold ssthresh = cwnd / 2, cwnd = ssthresh + 3 MSS, and enters Fast Recovery
questions.option_b: cwnd is reset to 1 MSS immediately
questions.explanation: Three duplicate ACKs signal a single lost segment without timeout; Reno sets ssthresh = cwnd/2, inflates cwnd by 3 for duplicate ACKs, and enters Fast Recovery.

questions.question_text: In the TCP Congestion Control mechanism, what triggers TCP to drop its congestion window (cwnd) immediately down to 1 Maximum Segment Size (MSS) in TCP Tahoe?
questions.option_b: A retransmission timeout (RTO)
questions.explanation: A timeout indicates severe network congestion, prompting TCP to reset cwnd to 1 MSS and re-enter slow start.

questions.question_text: What is Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange vulnerable to in the absence of authentication / certificates?
questions.option_b: Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attacks
questions.explanation: Without authentication (like digital certificates in TLS), an active attacker can establish independent DH exchanges with both endpoints.

questions.question_text: What is Head-of-Line (HoL) Blocking in HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3?
questions.option_a: HTTP/1.1 suffers HTTP-level HoL; HTTP/2 multiplexes streams but suffers TCP-level HoL; HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP to eliminate TCP HoL
questions.option_b: HTTP/3 introduces HoL blocking for security
questions.explanation: HTTP/2 multiplexes logical streams over a single TCP connection, so a single dropped TCP packet stalls all streams; HTTP/3 uses QUIC (UDP) so stream packet loss is independent.

questions.question_text: What is the Bandwidth-Delay Product (BDP) and what does it represent?
questions.option_b: Bandwidth * Round-Trip Time; the maximum data in flight required to fill the network pipe
questions.option_d: Transmission rate * Link distance; signal attenuation
questions.explanation: BDP = Bandwidth * RTT measures the maximum amount of unacknowledged data that can be in transit through the link at any moment.

questions.question_text: What is the Silly Window Syndrome in TCP and how is Clark's solution implemented?
questions.option_a: Sender transmits zero-length packets; receiver drops them
questions.option_b: Small segments exchanged repeatedly causing extreme overhead; Clark forces the receiver not to advertise small window increases until at least 1 MSS or half receive buffer is free
questions.option_c: Packets loop between two routers; solved by TTL
questions.explanation: Clark's solution prevents the receiver from advertising small window openings until min(MSS, buffer/2) space is available.

questions.question_text: What is the difference between Anycast, Unicast, Multicast, and Broadcast?
questions.option_a: Anycast delivers to the single nearest topological node among a group; Unicast to one; Multicast to a specific group; Broadcast to all nodes in the subnet
questions.option_b: Anycast delivers to all nodes in the world
questions.option_c: Broadcast routes across the global Internet
questions.explanation: Anycast shares an IP among multiple hosts and routes packets to the topologically closest host via BGP/IGP.

questions.question_text: What is the difference between TCP Tahoe and TCP Reno on packet loss detection?
questions.option_a: Tahoe resets cwnd to 1 MSS on both timeout and 3 dup ACKs; Reno resets cwnd to 1 on timeout but halves cwnd on 3 dup ACKs
questions.option_b: Tahoe does not support slow start
questions.option_c: Reno does not support sliding windows
questions.option_d: Tahoe supports selective acknowledgments whereas Reno does not
questions.explanation: Tahoe always drops cwnd back to 1 MSS; Reno introduced Fast Recovery to halve cwnd upon 3 duplicate ACKs without falling back to slow start.

questions.question_text: What is the key advantage of BBR (Bottleneck Bandwidth and RTT) congestion control over loss-based algorithms like CUBIC?
questions.option_a: BBR assumes any loss is a link failure
questions.option_b: BBR models network throughput and min RTT directly rather than interpreting packet loss as congestion, avoiding bufferbloat
questions.explanation: BBR regulates pacing rate based on estimated bottleneck bandwidth and minimum round-trip time, independent of packet loss.

questions.question_text: What role does Server Name Indication (SNI) play in TLS Handshake?
questions.option_a: It encrypts the client MAC address
questions.option_b: It allows a client to specify the target hostname during the ClientHello message before the server certificate is sent
questions.option_d: It negotiates TCP sliding window size
questions.explanation: SNI enables a single server/IP to host multiple secure SSL/TLS websites by letting the client state which virtual host certificate it expects.

questions.question_text: How does TCP achieve reliable data delivery?
questions.option_a: By using UDP as a fallback
questions.option_b: Sequence numbers, acknowledgments, checksums, and retransmissions upon timeout
questions.option_d: By broadcasting to all subnet hosts
questions.explanation: TCP numbers each byte sent, requires receiver ACKs, calculates checksums, and retransmits unacknowledged packets upon timeout.

questions.question_text: In TCP, what mechanism prevents a fast sender from overwhelming a slow receiver's buffer?
questions.option_b: Flow Control (Sliding Window)
questions.explanation: TCP Flow Control uses the advertised receive window (rwnd) to ensure the sender does not exceed the receiver's available buffer capacity.

questions.question_text: What does CSMA/CD stand for in Ethernet networking?
questions.option_a: Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection
questions.option_b: Channel Switching Multiple Access with Carrier Division
questions.option_c: Control System Message Allocation with Circuit Delivery
questions.option_d: Centralized Synchronous Media Access with Collision Deflection
questions.explanation: CSMA/CD listens before transmitting on shared half-duplex media and aborts transmission if a collision is detected.

questions.question_text: What does NAT (Network Address Translation) enable in IPv4 networks?
questions.option_a: Translating domain names to IP addresses
questions.option_b: Mapping private internal IP addresses to one or more public IP addresses
questions.explanation: NAT maps multiple private non-routable IP addresses (RFC 1918) to public IPs, conserving IPv4 address space.

questions.question_text: What does the Time to Live (TTL) field in an IPv4 packet header prevent?
questions.option_b: Packets from looping infinitely in the network
questions.explanation: Every router decrements the TTL by at least 1; if TTL reaches 0, the packet is discarded and an ICMP Time Exceeded message is sent back.

questions.question_text: What is SYN Flood attack and what mitigation is commonly deployed?
questions.option_a: A UDP reflection attack mitigated by DNSSEC
questions.option_b: A DoS attack consuming TCP connection slots mitigated by SYN Cookies
questions.option_c: A physical cable cut mitigated by STP
questions.option_d: A MAC spoofing attack mitigated by DHCP snooping
questions.explanation: SYN Flood overwhelms the half-open backlog queue; SYN cookies eliminate state storage until the final client ACK arrives.

questions.question_text: What is the maximum hop count allowed in Routing Information Protocol (RIP) before a route is considered unreachable?
questions.explanation: RIP uses 15 as the maximum valid metric; a hop count of 16 is defined as infinity / unreachable to limit counting-to-infinity loops.

questions.question_text: What is the maximum number of usable host IP addresses in a /24 IPv4 subnet?
questions.explanation: A /24 subnet has 2^(32-24) = 256 total addresses, minus 2 for network address (all 0s) and broadcast address (all 1s) = 254 usable hosts.

questions.question_text: What is the primary difference between Distance Vector (e.g. RIP) and Link State (e.g. OSPF) routing protocols?
questions.option_a: Distance vector uses Dijkstra; link state uses Bellman-Ford
questions.option_b: Distance vector shares routing table with neighbors; link state floods full topology info across the area
questions.option_c: Distance vector has no hop limit
questions.option_d: Link state cannot avoid routing loops
questions.explanation: Distance Vector protocols share vector distances with immediate neighbors (Bellman-Ford), while Link State protocols flood link states so every router knows the full graph topology (Dijkstra).

questions.question_text: What is the primary difference between TCP and UDP at the Transport layer?
questions.option_a: TCP is connectionless and unreliable; UDP is connection-oriented
questions.option_b: TCP provides reliable, sequenced data delivery with flow control; UDP is lightweight and connectionless
questions.option_c: TCP cannot detect errors, while UDP provides checksum recovery
questions.option_d: UDP guarantees packet delivery order without acknowledgments
questions.explanation: TCP establishes a 3-way handshake and handles acknowledgments, retransmissions, and flow control; UDP delivers packets with low overhead without connection state.

questions.question_text: What is the primary function of ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol)?
questions.option_b: Error reporting and diagnostic control messaging in IP networks
questions.explanation: ICMP communicates network layer error conditions (e.g. Destination Unreachable, Time Exceeded) and diagnostic queries (Echo/Ping).

questions.question_text: What is the purpose of the Spanning Tree Protocol (STP, IEEE 802.1D)?
questions.option_b: To prevent bridge loops and broadcast storms in redundant Layer 2 switched networks
questions.explanation: STP detects loops in switched Ethernet networks and disables redundant links, keeping only a loop-free tree active.

questions.question_text: What is the sequence of packets exchanged in the TCP 3-Way Handshake to establish a connection?
questions.option_b: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK
questions.explanation: The client sends SYN, the server responds with SYN-ACK, and the client finishes with ACK.

questions.question_text: Which HTTP status code indicates '301 Moved Permanently'?
questions.option_b: Permanent Redirect to a new URI
questions.explanation: HTTP 301 signifies that the target resource has been permanently assigned a new URI.

questions.question_text: Which protocol operates between Autonomous Systems (AS) on the global Internet backbone?
questions.option_b: RIP
questions.explanation: BGP is the standardized exterior gateway protocol designed to route traffic between distinct autonomous systems across the Internet.

questions.question_text: ACID stands for?
questions.option_b: Availability,Consistency,Isolation,Durability
questions.explanation: ACID ensures reliable DB transactions

questions.question_text: Foreign key?
questions.option_b: References PK of another table
questions.explanation: Foreign key enforces referential integrity

questions.question_text: Purpose of GROUP BY?
questions.option_b: Filter rows
questions.explanation: GROUP BY groups for aggregate operations

questions.question_text: TRUNCATE vs DELETE?
questions.option_b: TRUNCATE is faster, no row log
questions.explanation: TRUNCATE removes all rows without row-level logging

questions.question_text: What does DDL stand for in SQL?
questions.option_b: Data Distribution Logic
questions.explanation: DDL (Data Definition Language) includes commands like CREATE, ALTER, DROP, and TRUNCATE that define database schema structure.

questions.question_text: What does DML stand for in SQL?
questions.option_b: Data Manipulation Language
questions.explanation: DML (Data Manipulation Language) comprises commands such as SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE used for managing data within schema objects.

questions.question_text: What is a Primary Key in a relational database?
questions.option_a: A key that can contain duplicate values
questions.option_b: A column or set of columns that uniquely identifies each row in a table and cannot contain NULL values
questions.option_c: A key that links to another table
questions.option_d: An optional index created on text columns
questions.explanation: A primary key uniquely identifies each record in a relational table and enforces uniqueness and non-null constraints.

questions.question_text: What type of integrity constraint ensures that a foreign key value must match an existing primary key in the parent table or be NULL?
questions.option_b: Referential Integrity
questions.explanation: Referential integrity guarantees that foreign keys maintain valid relationships pointing to existing parent records.

questions.question_text: Which JOIN returns all rows from both tables?
questions.option_b: LEFT JOIN
questions.explanation: FULL OUTER JOIN returns all rows

questions.question_text: Which SQL aggregate function calculates the total sum of numeric values in a column?
questions.option_b: SUM()
questions.explanation: SUM() returns the arithmetic sum of all non-null values in a given column.

questions.question_text: Which SQL clause is used to filter records returned by a SELECT query?
questions.option_b: WHERE
questions.explanation: The WHERE clause filters rows based on specified search conditions before grouping.

questions.question_text: Which SQL command is used to modify existing data within a table?
questions.option_b: UPDATE
questions.explanation: The UPDATE statement modifies values in existing rows of a table based on an optional condition.

questions.question_text: Which SQL command is used to permanently remove all rows from a table without logging individual row deletions?
questions.option_b: DROP
questions.explanation: TRUNCATE is a DDL command that deallocates data pages directly, making it much faster and non-row-logged compared to DELETE.

questions.question_text: Which SQL statement is used to insert new records into a database table?
questions.option_b: INSERT INTO
questions.explanation: The INSERT INTO statement adds one or more new rows into a database table.

questions.question_text: Which normal form eliminates partial dependencies?
questions.option_b: 2NF
questions.explanation: 2NF removes partial dependencies

questions.question_text: Consider two concurrent transactions T1 and T2. Under Strict 2-Phase Locking (Strict 2PL), when are exclusive locks released?
questions.option_a: As soon as the item is no longer referenced
questions.option_b: Immediately after the transaction enters the shrinking phase
questions.option_c: Only after the transaction commits or aborts
questions.option_d: Whenever a shared lock request arrives
questions.explanation: Strict 2PL prevents cascading rollbacks (cascadeless schedules) by holding all exclusive write locks until the transaction completes (commit or abort).

questions.question_text: How is deadlock detected dynamically in DBMS lock managers?
questions.option_b: By maintaining a Wait-For Graph (WFG) and detecting cycles
questions.explanation: A Wait-For Graph directs an edge from Ti to Tj if Ti is waiting for a lock held by Tj; a directed cycle in the WFG indicates a deadlock.

questions.question_text: In Write-Ahead Logging (WAL), what are the STEAL and NO-FORCE buffer pool management policies?
questions.option_a: STEAL allows uncommitted buffer pages to be written to disk; NO-FORCE means committed pages need not be immediately flushed to disk upon commit
questions.option_b: STEAL forces all dirty pages to disk immediately
questions.option_d: STEAL prevents transactions from modifying cached buffers
questions.explanation: STEAL permits writing dirty uncommitted pages to free RAM (requiring UNDO logging); NO-FORCE defers flushing committed pages to disk (requiring REDO logging).

questions.question_text: In a B+ Tree index of order m, what is the maximum number of keys in an internal node?
questions.explanation: In a B+ tree of order m, an internal node can have at most m child pointers and therefore at most m - 1 keys separating them.

questions.question_text: In database recovery, what does the ARIES recovery algorithm use to ensure idempotence during REDO phase?
questions.option_b: Page LSN (Log Sequence Number)
questions.explanation: ARIES compares the log record's LSN with the PageLSN recorded on disk: if PageLSN >= LSN, the update is already reflected and REDO is skipped.

questions.question_text: In distributed transactions, how does the Two-Phase Commit (2PC) protocol handle a coordinator crash during the prepare phase?
questions.option_b: Participants who voted YES are blocked until the coordinator recovers or an election elects a new coordinator
questions.option_d: Database automatically switches to single-node mode
questions.explanation: 2PC is a blocking protocol: if the coordinator crashes after participants vote YES but before sending COMMIT/ABORT, participants must wait synchronously.

questions.question_text: In write-ahead logging (WAL), when can a transaction T write a modified dirty page to disk?
questions.option_b: Only after the log record describing the update is flushed to non-volatile storage
questions.option_c: Only after all transactions in the system commit
questions.option_d: Only when the checkpoint background daemon triggers
questions.explanation: The fundamental invariant of WAL states that the log record detailing an update must reach persistent disk before the corresponding modified data page is written to disk.

questions.question_text: Under the Two-Phase Locking (2PL) protocol, what guarantees conflict serializability?
questions.option_b: A transaction cannot acquire any new lock once it releases any lock (Growing phase followed by Shrinking phase)
questions.option_c: All read locks must be converted to exclusive locks
questions.option_d: Transactions must declare all resources at compile time
questions.explanation: Basic 2PL states that once a transaction releases a lock (shrinking phase), it cannot acquire any further locks, which prevents cycles in the precedence graph.

questions.question_text: What constitutes 4th Normal Form (4NF) in relational databases?
questions.option_a: A table in BCNF that contains no non-trivial multivalued dependencies (MVD)
questions.option_b: A table with no foreign keys
questions.option_c: A table with at most 4 columns
questions.option_d: A table where all attributes are atomic integers
questions.explanation: 4NF requires BCNF and eliminates non-trivial multivalued dependencies X ->> Y where X is not a superkey.

questions.question_text: What is Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC) and what is its primary benefit?
questions.option_a: It locks tables at row level only
questions.option_b: It creates versions of data items on update so that readers do not block writers and writers do not block readers
questions.option_c: It prevents all deadlock scenarios in distributed systems
questions.explanation: MVCC provides snapshot isolation where readers see consistent historical snapshots without acquiring read locks, eliminating reader-writer lock contention.

questions.question_text: What is Phantom Read phenomenon and what lock mechanism prevents it in SQL databases?
questions.option_a: A query reads deleted memory addresses; prevented by mutex
questions.option_b: A query with a range condition (e.g. salary > 50000) sees new matching rows inserted by a concurrent transaction; prevented by Predicate Locks or Next-Key Locking
questions.option_c: A server crash that causes phantom data
questions.option_d: A corrupted index page; prevented by checksums
questions.explanation: Phantom reads occur when a transaction re-executes a range query and discovers newly inserted tuples satisfying the predicate; Next-Key locking in B+ trees prevents this.

questions.question_text: What is the CAP Theorem for distributed data stores?
questions.option_a: Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance cannot all be simultaneously guaranteed in the presence of network partitions
questions.option_b: Concurrency, Atomicity, Performance must be balanced
questions.option_d: Clustering, Auditing, Profiling are mutually exclusive
questions.explanation: Eric Brewer's CAP theorem states that a distributed system must choose between Consistency (CP) and Availability (AP) during network partitions.

questions.question_text: What is the difference between Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC) and Pessimistic Locking?
questions.option_a: OCC acquires locks upfront; Pessimistic does not use locks
questions.option_b: OCC validates conflicts at commit time assuming collisions are rare; Pessimistic acquires locks prior to reading/writing assuming conflicts are common
questions.option_c: OCC is used only in NoSQL databases
questions.option_d: Pessimistic locking does not support ACID properties
questions.explanation: OCC operates in three phases (Read, Validation, Write) without locking data during execution, which outperforms pessimistic locking in low-contention workloads.

questions.question_text: What is the difference between Strict 2PL and Rigorous 2PL?
questions.option_a: Strict 2PL holds exclusive locks until commit/abort; Rigorous 2PL holds BOTH shared and exclusive locks until commit/abort
questions.option_b: Strict 2PL permits dirty reads
questions.option_c: Rigorous 2PL does not prevent cascading aborts
questions.option_d: Strict 2PL uses timestamps instead of locks
questions.explanation: Strict 2PL releases shared locks during shrinking phase but holds exclusive locks until end of transaction; Rigorous 2PL holds all locks until termination.

questions.question_text: What is the purpose of Checkpointing in database recovery systems?
questions.option_b: To periodically flush dirty buffer pool pages to disk and write a checkpoint record, bounding the log volume scanned during recovery
questions.explanation: Checkpoints flush dirty pages and log records, guaranteeing that transactions committed prior to the checkpoint do not need to be reprocessed from the beginning of the log.

questions.question_text: A relation is in Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF) if and only if for every non-trivial functional dependency X -> Y:
questions.option_b: X is a superkey
questions.option_c: X is a candidate key and Y is prime
questions.explanation: BCNF requires that for every non-trivial functional dependency X -> Y, the determinant X must strictly be a superkey.

questions.question_text: HAVING clause does?
questions.option_b: Filter after GROUP BY
questions.explanation: HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY

questions.question_text: In relational database transaction processing, which isolation level prevents 'Dirty Read' and 'Non-repeatable Read', but may still allow 'Phantom Reads'?
questions.option_b: Read Committed
questions.explanation: Repeatable Read locks rows queried during a transaction preventing updates, but does not block inserts of new matching rows (phantoms).

questions.question_text: What dependency is eliminated in 3rd Normal Form (3NF)?
questions.option_b: Transitive functional dependency of non-prime attributes on candidate keys
questions.explanation: 3NF requires 2NF plus no transitive dependencies between non-prime attributes and the primary/candidate key.

questions.question_text: What dependency must be eliminated for a relation to be in 2nd Normal Form (2NF)?
questions.option_b: Partial functional dependency on a composite candidate key
questions.explanation: 2NF requires the relation to be in 1NF and have no non-prime attribute partially dependent on any candidate key.

questions.question_text: What does a Self JOIN achieve in SQL?
questions.option_a: Joins a table to an external CSV file
questions.option_b: Joins a table to itself by aliasing it as two distinct table references
questions.option_c: Automatically merges all rows with identical column names
questions.explanation: A self-join joins a relation with itself (e.g. employee reporting to manager within the same employees table).

questions.question_text: What is a 'Non-Repeatable Read' phenomenon?
questions.option_a: A query fails to execute twice
questions.option_b: A transaction reads the same row twice and observes different values because another transaction committed an update in between
questions.option_d: A table scan that misses newly inserted rows
questions.explanation: Non-repeatable reads happen when re-reading a row within a transaction yields modified data committed by another transaction.

questions.question_text: What is a candidate key in relational database design?
questions.option_b: A minimal superkey capable of uniquely identifying a tuple without redundant attributes
questions.option_c: A key composed of all columns in a table
questions.option_d: A foreign key referencing a parent table
questions.explanation: A candidate key is a minimal set of attributes that uniquely identifies tuples in a relation; one candidate key is chosen as primary key.

questions.question_text: What is a clustered index in a relational database?
questions.option_a: An index that alters the physical storage order of rows in the table
questions.option_b: An index stored in a separate memory table
questions.option_c: An index that permits duplicate keys only
questions.option_d: An index that cannot be created on primary keys
questions.explanation: A clustered index defines the physical order in which table rows are stored on disk; therefore, only one clustered index can exist per table.

questions.question_text: What is an index seek vs an index scan in query execution?
questions.option_a: Index seek navigates B+ Tree directly to matching rows; index scan traverses the entire index leaf sequence
questions.option_b: Index seek reads every page on disk
questions.option_c: Index scan is always faster than index seek
questions.option_d: Index seek applies only to non-indexed columns
questions.explanation: Index Seek uses the B+ Tree search tree to jump directly to qualified keys (O(log N)), whereas Index Scan reads all index pages sequentially.

questions.question_text: What is the difference between UNION and UNION ALL in SQL?
questions.option_a: UNION includes duplicates; UNION ALL removes duplicates
questions.option_b: UNION removes duplicate rows and sorts the result; UNION ALL retains all duplicates without sorting
questions.option_c: UNION works on single tables only
questions.option_d: UNION ALL is not valid SQL
questions.explanation: UNION performs a distinct operation to eliminate duplicates, while UNION ALL simply concatenates result sets, making it much faster.

questions.question_text: What is the phenomenon called 'Dirty Read' in database transactions?
questions.option_a: Reading data that is outdated by more than 1 hour
questions.option_b: A transaction reads uncommitted modifications made by another concurrent transaction
questions.option_c: Reading from a damaged disk block
questions.explanation: A dirty read occurs when Transaction A reads data modified by Transaction B before Transaction B has committed; if B aborts, the data is invalid.

questions.question_text: What is the primary difference between WHERE and HAVING clauses in SQL?
questions.option_a: WHERE filters before GROUP BY aggregation; HAVING filters after grouping
questions.option_b: HAVING can only be used with subqueries
questions.option_c: WHERE can only compare string values
questions.option_d: There is no difference; they are interchangeable
questions.explanation: WHERE filters individual rows before aggregation occurs; HAVING filters grouped rows based on aggregate function values.

questions.question_text: What is the primary reason B+ Trees are preferred over Binary Search Trees for disk-based database indexes?
questions.option_a: B+ Trees have larger branching factors, minimizing expensive disk I/O operations
questions.option_b: B+ Trees use less RAM
questions.option_c: Binary search trees cannot handle numeric data
questions.option_d: B+ Trees do not require rebalancing
questions.explanation: B+ Trees have high fan-out (order m), resulting in very shallow depth (typically 3-4 levels) and sequential leaf node linking for range scans.

questions.question_text: Which SQL transaction isolation level prevents Dirty Reads, Non-Repeatable Reads, and Phantom Reads?
questions.option_b: Read Committed
questions.explanation: Serializable is the highest ANSI SQL isolation level, preventing dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantom reads.

questions.question_text: In a Min-Heap, where is the minimum element always located?
questions.option_b: At the root node (index 0)
questions.explanation: The min-heap property ensures that every parent is smaller than or equal to its children, placing the global minimum at the root.

questions.question_text: What happens when you attempt to pop from an empty Stack?
questions.option_b: Stack Underflow
questions.explanation: Popping or peeking from an empty stack results in a stack underflow condition.

questions.question_text: What is a Binary Heap typically represented as in memory?
questions.option_b: A flat 1D array where children of node i are at 2i+1 and 2i+2
questions.explanation: Because a binary heap is a complete binary tree, it can be compactly stored in a contiguous 1D array without pointer overhead.

questions.question_text: What is a circular queue primarily used to prevent in array-based queue implementations?
questions.option_b: Wasted memory space when elements are dequeued from the front while rear reaches the array end
questions.explanation: A circular queue wraps front and rear indices using modulo arithmetic, reusing freed front slots without shifting elements.

questions.question_text: What is a major advantage of a Doubly Linked List over a Singly Linked List?
questions.option_b: It allows bidirectional traversal (both forward and backward) and O(1) deletion given a node pointer
questions.explanation: Having both 'next' and 'prev' pointers permits moving both directions and splicing out a given node in O(1) without knowing its predecessor.

questions.question_text: What is the average time complexity of key lookup in a Hash Table with a well-designed hash function?
questions.option_b: O(log N)
questions.explanation: A uniform hash function with appropriate load factor distributes keys evenly across buckets, achieving O(1) average lookup.

questions.question_text: What is the primary difference between a Singly Linked List and an Array?
questions.option_a: Arrays have dynamic size; linked lists have fixed size
questions.option_b: Arrays have contiguous memory allocation with O(1) indexing; linked lists use non-contiguous nodes linked by pointers with O(N) indexing
questions.explanation: Arrays store elements contiguously allowing direct index arithmetic; linked lists scatter nodes across heap memory connected via pointers.

questions.question_text: What is the time complexity of searching for an element in an unsorted Singly Linked List of size N?
questions.option_b: O(log N)
questions.explanation: Because nodes are linked sequentially and cannot be indexed directly, sequential traversal takes O(N) worst-case time.

questions.question_text: What is the time complexity of the peek() operation on a Stack or Queue?
questions.option_b: O(log N)
questions.explanation: Peek simply inspects the top/front element without removing it, taking constant O(1) time.

questions.question_text: What is the time complexity to insert a new node at the beginning of a Singly Linked List given the head pointer?
questions.option_b: O(log N)
questions.explanation: Prepending to a linked list involves creating a node, pointing its next pointer to head, and updating head in O(1) time.

questions.question_text: Which data structure is best suited for evaluating postfix arithmetic expressions?
questions.option_b: Stack
questions.explanation: Operands are pushed onto a stack; upon encountering an operator, the two top operands are popped, evaluated, and the result is pushed back.

questions.question_text: Which operation on a Queue removes an element from the front?
questions.option_b: dequeue
questions.explanation: The dequeue operation removes and returns the element at the front of the queue.

questions.question_text: Which operation on a Stack adds a new element to the top?
questions.option_b: push
questions.explanation: The push operation places a new item onto the top of the stack.

questions.question_text: Which principle does a Stack data structure follow?
questions.option_b: LIFO (Last In, First Out)
questions.explanation: A stack operates on the Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) principle, where insertions and deletions happen only at the top.

questions.question_text: Which principle does a standard Queue data structure follow?
questions.option_b: FIFO (First In, First Out)
questions.explanation: A queue follows First-In, First-Out (FIFO), where elements are enqueued at the rear and dequeued from the front.

questions.question_text: In Cuckoo Hashing, what mechanism guarantees O(1) worst-case lookup time?
questions.option_a: Multiple linked lists at each slot
questions.option_b: Each key can only reside in one of two specific locations determined by two distinct hash functions h1(k) and h2(k)
questions.explanation: Because an item can only ever be in bucket h1(x) or h2(x), lookup requires checking at most 2 array locations, guaranteeing strict O(1) worst-case search.

questions.question_text: What are the structural invariants of a Red-Black Tree?
questions.option_a: Root is black; leaves (NIL) are black; if a node is red, both children are black; every path from a node to descendant leaves contains the same number of black nodes
questions.option_b: Left subtree height equals right subtree height strictly
questions.option_c: All keys must be prime numbers
questions.option_d: Every node must have at least 3 children
questions.explanation: These 5 properties guarantee that no path from root to leaf is more than twice as long as any other, keeping tree height <= 2 * log2(N + 1).

questions.question_text: What is a B-Tree of minimum degree t (order 2t) and what is the property of non-root internal nodes?
questions.option_a: Every non-root node must contain at least t-1 keys and at most 2t-1 keys, and all leaves are at the exact same depth
questions.option_b: Every node has at most 2 keys
questions.option_c: Leaves can be at any depth
questions.explanation: B-Tree invariants ensure balanced height by requiring all non-root nodes to have between t-1 and 2t-1 keys, keeping disk reads bounded to O(log_t N).

questions.question_text: What is a Bloom Filter and what are its false-positive and false-negative properties?
questions.option_a: Guarantees zero false positives and zero false negatives
questions.option_b: A space-efficient probabilistic data structure that can yield false positives but NEVER false negatives
questions.option_c: A hash set that produces false negatives but no false positives
questions.option_d: An encrypted data structure for secure hash tables
questions.explanation: A Bloom filter uses k hash functions on a bit array; if any bit is 0, the item is definitely absent (no false negatives), but collisions can produce false positives.

questions.question_text: What is a Cartesian Tree built from an array of numbers?
questions.option_a: A tree satisfying BST property on array indices and Min/Max-Heap property on array values
questions.option_b: A tree where every node has coordinates (x, y)
questions.option_c: A geometric convex hull represented as a DAG
questions.option_d: A tree used exclusively for matrix multiplication
questions.explanation: In a Cartesian tree, inorder traversal yields the original array index order, while parent-child relations satisfy the heap property on array values (used in RMQ).

questions.question_text: What is a Fenwick Tree (Binary Indexed Tree) and what does parent index 'i - (i & -i)' compute?
questions.option_a: The index of the left sibling in a complete binary tree
questions.option_b: The index of the parent responsible for the next prefix sum range by removing the lowest set bit
questions.option_c: The square root of index i
questions.option_d: The hash code of index i
questions.explanation: The expression i & -i isolates the least significant set bit; subtracting it moves to the ancestor containing the remainder of the prefix sum.

questions.question_text: What is a K-D Tree (K-Dimensional Tree) primarily used for?
questions.option_b: Organizing points in a k-dimensional space for efficient spatial searches such as Nearest Neighbor and Range Queries
questions.option_c: Distributing network packets across K routers
questions.option_d: Balancing AVL trees with K rotations
questions.explanation: A k-d tree partitions k-dimensional space by cycling through coordinate axes at each depth level, speeding up nearest-neighbor search.

questions.question_text: What is a Persistent Data Structure?
questions.option_a: A data structure saved to a database table on disk
questions.option_b: A data structure that preserves previous versions of itself when modified, allowing access to historical snapshots
questions.option_c: A data structure that never frees allocated RAM
questions.option_d: A data structure immune to power loss
questions.explanation: Persistent data structures (e.g. purely functional trees) use node-copying and path-copying to produce new versions sharing unchanged subtrees with older versions.

questions.question_text: What is a Segment Tree with Lazy Propagation and why is Lazy Propagation needed?
questions.option_a: To delay tree construction until user queries arrive
questions.option_b: To update a whole range of size N in O(log N) time by deferring updates to children nodes until they are visited
questions.option_c: To convert recursive trees into iterative arrays
questions.option_d: To reduce space complexity from O(4N) to O(N)
questions.explanation: Lazy propagation stores pending updates in a lazy tag at parent nodes, avoiding O(N) traversal of all descendants and keeping range updates O(log N).

questions.question_text: What is a Skip List and what are its average time complexities for search, insertion, and deletion?
questions.option_a: A linked list that skips every second element; O(N) operations
questions.option_b: A probabilistic multi-level linked list with express lanes; O(log N) average time for search, insert, and delete with O(N) space
questions.option_c: A stack that skips popped items; O(1) operations
questions.option_d: A binary search tree flattened into an array
questions.explanation: Skip lists use randomized coin flips to build layered linked lists that provide O(log N) average search/insert/delete without complex tree rotations.

questions.question_text: What is a Splay Tree and what operation is performed on every access?
questions.option_a: Nodes are sorted using bubble sort
questions.option_b: The accessed node is brought to the root via a series of tree rotations (splaying: zig, zig-zig, zig-zag), achieving O(log N) amortized operations
questions.option_c: The root is deleted and recreated
questions.option_d: The tree is balanced using Euler tours
questions.explanation: Splaying moves accessed keys to the root, guaranteeing O(log N) amortized performance and near O(1) access for frequently referenced elements.

questions.question_text: What is a Treap (Tree-Heap) data structure?
questions.option_a: A binary search tree where each node has a key satisfying BST invariant and a randomized priority satisfying Heap invariant
questions.option_b: A trie combined with a min-heap
questions.option_c: A tournament tree used for external merge sort
questions.explanation: A Treap maintains BST order on keys and max/min-heap order on randomly generated priorities, achieving expected O(log N) balanced tree height.

questions.question_text: What is the amortized time complexity of the 'find' and 'union' operations in a Disjoint Set Union (DSU) data structure with Union by Rank and Path Compression?
questions.option_b: O(log N)
questions.option_c: O(alpha(N)) where alpha is the Inverse Ackermann function
questions.explanation: Combining path compression with union by rank/size reduces the amortized cost per operation to O(alpha(N)), which is <= 4 for all practical values.

questions.question_text: What is the time complexity of range sum queries in a 2D Fenwick Tree of size M x N?
questions.option_b: O(log M * log N)
questions.explanation: A 2D BIT nests bitwise manipulations across two dimensions, executing updates and prefix sums in O(log M * log N) time.

questions.question_text: What is the time complexity of the decrease-key operation in a Fibonacci Heap vs a Binary Heap?
questions.option_a: Binary Heap: O(log N); Fibonacci Heap: O(1) amortized
questions.option_b: Binary Heap: O(1); Fibonacci Heap: O(log N)
questions.option_d: Both are O(log N) worst case
questions.explanation: Fibonacci Heaps achieve O(1) amortized decrease-key via lazy cascading cuts, which is why they improve Dijkstra's theoretical bound to O(E + V log V).

questions.question_text: How can a Queue be implemented using TWO Stacks?
questions.option_a: By pushing to stack1, and popping from stack2 (transferring stack1 to stack2 only when stack2 is empty)
questions.option_b: By pushing to both stacks simultaneously
questions.option_c: By reversing the first stack on every single enqueue
questions.option_d: It is theoretically impossible to implement a queue using stacks
questions.explanation: Stack1 buffers enqueues; when dequeue is requested, stack2 pops if non-empty, otherwise stack1 is dumped into stack2 reversing order (amortized O(1)).

questions.question_text: What is Open Addressing in Hash Tables and which probing sequence checks buckets at indices (hash + i^2) % M?
questions.option_b: Quadratic Probing
questions.explanation: Quadratic probing offsets the probe index quadratically (c1*i + c2*i^2), reducing primary clustering found in linear probing.

questions.question_text: What is a Circular Linked List?
questions.option_a: A linked list with no data elements
questions.option_b: A linked list where the last node's next pointer points back to the first node (head) instead of NULL
questions.option_c: A linked list arranged in a circle on screen
questions.option_d: A linked list with multiple head pointers
questions.explanation: In a circular linked list, the final node references head, enabling continuous cyclic traversal through all nodes.

questions.question_text: What is a Deque (Double-Ended Queue)?
questions.option_a: A queue that supports only integer data
questions.option_b: A linear data structure allowing insertion and deletion at both ends (front and rear) in O(1) time
questions.option_c: A queue with two parallel consumer threads
questions.option_d: A priority queue implemented with an array
questions.explanation: A deque supports push_front, push_back, pop_front, and pop_back all in amortized O(1) time.

questions.question_text: What is a Monotonic Stack primarily used for in algorithmic problem solving?
questions.option_b: Finding the Next Greater Element (NGE) or Previous Smaller Element in O(N) total time
questions.explanation: A monotonic stack keeps elements in monotonic order, popping elements that violate the invariant to solve range boundary problems in O(N).

questions.question_text: What is a Self-Organizing List and how does the 'Move-To-Front' (MTF) heuristic work?
questions.option_a: The list is sorted using quicksort periodically
questions.option_b: Whenever an element is accessed, it is moved to the head of the list to accelerate subsequent accesses to popular items
questions.option_c: Elements are deleted if not accessed within 1 minute
questions.option_d: The list maintains half of its elements in an array
questions.explanation: Move-to-Front exploits temporal locality by placing accessed items at the head, achieving competitive online search performance.

questions.question_text: What is an XOR Linked List (Memory Efficient Doubly Linked List)?
questions.option_a: A linked list that stores data encrypted with XOR cipher
questions.option_b: A doubly linked list where each node stores the XOR of previous and next node memory addresses in a single pointer field
questions.option_c: A list that supports only bitwise operations
questions.option_d: A linked list with cycle detection built in
questions.explanation: By storing address(prev) XOR address(next) in one pointer field, an XOR linked list achieves two-way traversal using half the pointer memory.

questions.question_text: What is collision resolution by 'Separate Chaining' in Hash Tables?
questions.option_a: Probing the next available array slot sequentially
questions.option_b: Maintaining a linked list or balanced tree of colliding entries at each bucket index
questions.option_c: Resizing the array by factor 2 immediately upon any collision
questions.option_d: Hashing the key a second time using another hash function
questions.explanation: Separate chaining places all key-value pairs that hash to the same bucket index into a linked list or secondary tree at that bucket.

questions.question_text: What is the difference between a Complete Binary Tree and a Full Binary Tree?
questions.option_a: A full binary tree has all leaves at the same depth; a complete tree does not
questions.option_b: In a full binary tree every node has 0 or 2 children; in a complete binary tree all levels are completely filled except possibly the last which is filled from left to right
questions.option_c: Complete binary trees cannot have more than 7 nodes
questions.option_d: Full trees are always binary search trees
questions.explanation: Full (proper) binary trees require every internal node to have exactly two children; complete trees pack all levels tightly from left to right.

questions.question_text: What is the load factor (alpha) of a Hash Table with N elements and M buckets?
questions.option_b: N / M
questions.explanation: Load factor alpha = N / M measures the average number of items per bucket; resizing typically triggers when alpha exceeds ~0.75.

questions.question_text: What is the time complexity of the build_heap (heapify) operation to construct a Binary Heap from an unsorted array of size N?
questions.option_b: O(N)
questions.explanation: Sifting down from the lowest internal nodes upward sums to N * sum(h / 2^h) = O(N), achieving linear construction time.

questions.question_text: What is the time complexity to detect a cycle in a Singly Linked List using Floyd's Tortoise and Hare algorithm?
questions.option_b: O(N) time, O(1) space
questions.explanation: Moving slow by 1 step and fast by 2 steps detects cycles in linear O(N) time while utilizing strictly O(1) auxiliary memory.

questions.question_text: What is the time complexity to find the intersection point of two Singly Linked Lists of lengths M and N?
questions.option_b: O(M + N)
questions.explanation: Traversing both lists with two pointers and wrapping to the head of the other upon reaching NULL aligns distances in O(M + N) time and O(1) space.

questions.question_text: What is the time complexity to insert a new element into a Binary Heap of size N?
questions.option_b: O(log N)
questions.explanation: Insertion places the element at the end and sifts it up along the tree height, taking at most O(log N) comparisons/swaps.

questions.question_text: What is the worst-case time complexity of lookup in a Hash Table that resolves collisions using Separate Chaining?
questions.option_b: O(log N)
questions.explanation: If a degenerate hash function maps all N keys to the exact same bucket, the bucket's linked list degrades search to O(N).

questions.question_text: Can an abstract class be instantiated directly with the 'new' keyword?
questions.option_b: No, never
questions.option_c: Only if it has no abstract methods
questions.option_d: Only if it is marked public
questions.explanation: Abstract classes cannot be instantiated directly; they must be subclassed with concrete implementations for all abstract methods.

questions.question_text: Method overloading means?
questions.option_b: Same name different params
questions.explanation: Overloading=same name,different signatures

questions.question_text: What is Encapsulation in Object-Oriented Programming?
questions.option_a: Hiding internal data and binding data with functions that manipulate it using private access specifiers
questions.option_b: Creating multiple methods with the same name
questions.option_c: Allowing a class to have multiple parents
questions.explanation: Encapsulation bundles data members and methods into a single class and restricts direct external access via access modifiers.

questions.question_text: What is a Constructor in OOP?
questions.option_a: A special method invoked automatically when an object is instantiated to initialize its state
questions.option_b: A method used to delete objects from RAM
questions.option_c: A static function used for math calculations
questions.option_d: A function that has no return value and cannot accept arguments
questions.explanation: Constructors initialize newly created object instances and typically share the class name.

questions.question_text: What is a Destructor in C++?
questions.option_a: A method called right before an object's memory is deallocated to release acquired resources
questions.option_b: A function that terminates the OS process
questions.option_d: A method that sets variables to NULL
questions.explanation: Destructors (~ClassName) clean up resources (file handles, memory) when an object goes out of scope or is deleted.

questions.question_text: What is an instance of a class called?
questions.option_b: Function
questions.explanation: An object is a concrete instance of a class containing its own state and allocated memory.

questions.question_text: What is method overloading (compile-time polymorphism)?
questions.option_a: Defining multiple methods in the same class with identical names but different parameter lists
questions.option_b: Redefining superclass methods with identical signatures
questions.option_d: Converting an object to an interface
questions.explanation: Method overloading allows multiple methods to share the same name with different signatures (parameter types/counts), resolved at compile time.

questions.question_text: What is method overriding in OOP?
questions.option_a: Defining multiple methods with the same name but different parameters in the same class
questions.option_b: A subclass providing a specific implementation of a method that is already defined in its superclass
questions.option_c: Calling private methods from another package
questions.explanation: Method overriding occurs when a subclass redefines an inherited virtual/instance method with the same signature.

questions.question_text: What is the default access modifier for members of a C++ class?
questions.option_b: private
questions.explanation: In C++, members of a class default to private, whereas members of a struct default to public.

questions.question_text: Which OOP concept allows a class to inherit properties and methods from another class?
questions.option_b: Inheritance
questions.explanation: Inheritance is the mechanism by which one class acquires the fields and methods of another class (superclass/base class).

questions.question_text: Which OOP feature allows treating derived class objects as if they were instances of their base class?
questions.option_b: Polymorphism
questions.explanation: Polymorphism enables uniform treatment of distinct derived types through base class pointers or references.

questions.question_text: Which OOP principle allows a subclass to provide a specific implementation of a method that is already defined in its superclass?
questions.option_b: Method Overriding (Polymorphism)
questions.explanation: Method overriding allows a derived class to customize behavior defined in the parent class using dynamic dispatch polymorphism.

questions.question_text: Which OOP principle hides implementation?
questions.option_b: Polymorphism
questions.explanation: Encapsulation hides internal state

questions.question_text: Which access modifier allows class members to be accessed only within the same class?
questions.option_b: protected
questions.explanation: Private members are accessible only within the body of the declaring class.

questions.question_text: Which keyword is used in C++ and Java to refer to the current instance of the class?
questions.option_b: this
questions.explanation: The 'this' keyword refers to the current invoking object instance in C++, Java, and C#.

questions.question_text: How does the Bridge Design Pattern decouple abstraction from implementation?
questions.option_a: By putting abstraction and implementation into separate inheritance hierarchies connected via an association pointer (composition)
questions.option_b: By merging all interfaces into one abstract class
questions.option_c: By compiling implementations into shared libraries at runtime
questions.explanation: Bridge replaces multi-dimensional inheritance growth with two independent hierarchies: the abstraction and the implementor, linked by composition.

questions.question_text: In C++, what is object slicing?
questions.option_a: Splitting an object across multiple CPU caches
questions.option_b: When a derived class object is assigned to a base class value object, copying only base members and stripping away derived state and virtual behavior
questions.option_c: Dividing an array of objects into chunks
questions.explanation: Assigning by value (Base b = derived;) slices off the derived portion, retaining only the Base subobject and destroying polymorphic behavior.

questions.question_text: What is Covariant Return Type in the context of method overriding?
questions.option_a: An overriding method in a derived class can return a more specific (derived) type than the method in the base class
questions.option_b: An overridden method can return any unrelated type
questions.option_c: Return types must always be strictly identical in all languages
questions.explanation: Covariance permits an overridden method to return a subtype of the return type declared in the superclass method without violating type safety.

questions.question_text: What is RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization) in C++?
questions.option_b: A programming idiom where resource lifecycle is bound to object lifetime; constructor acquires, destructor releases
questions.option_c: A rule that requires all variables to be global
questions.explanation: RAII guarantees exception-safe resource management (memory, file descriptors, mutex locks) by tying cleanup to deterministic destructor invocation upon stack unwinding.

questions.question_text: What is the Curiously Recurring Template Pattern (CRTP) in C++ and what is its primary benefit?
questions.option_a: A class inherits from a template instantiation of itself (class D : public B<D>); enables static polymorphism without vtable overhead
questions.option_b: A recursive function that parses XML tags
questions.option_c: A pattern that replaces all virtual destructors with macros
questions.option_d: A technique to dynamically allocate templates at runtime
questions.explanation: CRTP allows compile-time polymorphism (static dispatch) and code reuse without the runtime overhead of virtual functions (no vptr/vtable lookup).

questions.question_text: What is the Double-Checked Locking pattern for Singleton implementation, and why does the instance pointer require the 'volatile' keyword in Java/C++11?
questions.option_a: To allow multiple threads to create separate instances
questions.option_b: To prevent instruction reordering where a thread observes a non-null pointer before object construction completes
questions.explanation: Without volatile/memory barriers, compiler and CPU instruction reordering can publish the object pointer before constructor fields are initialized, leading to threads reading half-initialized objects.

questions.question_text: What is the Flyweight Design Pattern used for?
questions.option_a: To create lightweight threads for asynchronous execution
questions.option_b: To minimize memory usage by sharing common intrinsic state across a large number of fine-grained objects
questions.option_d: To dynamically change an object's class at runtime
questions.explanation: Flyweight separates intrinsic (shared, invariant) state from extrinsic (context-dependent) state, enabling millions of objects (e.g. text characters) to share minimal memory.

questions.question_text: What is the Law of Demeter (Principle of Least Knowledge)?
questions.option_a: A module should know about the complete internal details of all collaborating objects
questions.option_b: A method should only call methods of its own class, parameters, objects it creates, or its direct component fields (don't talk to strangers)
questions.option_c: All classes must have fewer than 10 methods
questions.option_d: Objects should never pass messages across threads
questions.explanation: The Law of Demeter discourages chain calls like a.getB().getC().doSomething(), reducing coupling between distant components.

questions.question_text: What is the Memento Design Pattern used for?
questions.option_a: Recording logs to disk in XML format
questions.option_b: Capturing and externalizing an object's internal state without violating encapsulation, enabling rollback/undo operations
questions.option_c: Generating unique UUIDs for database objects
questions.explanation: Memento stores an object's internal state snapshot (Originator creates Memento, stored by Caretaker) to restore state later without exposing private members.

questions.question_text: What is the difference between the Abstract Factory pattern and the Factory Method pattern?
questions.option_a: Factory Method uses inheritance and relies on a derived class method to instantiate a single product; Abstract Factory uses composition to create entire families of related products
questions.option_b: Factory Method creates interfaces; Abstract Factory creates classes
questions.option_c: There is no difference in modern UML
questions.option_d: Abstract Factory cannot instantiate concrete objects
questions.explanation: Factory Method defines an interface for creating an individual object; Abstract Factory is an object providing methods to create families of related or dependent objects.

questions.question_text: What is the fragile base class problem in object-oriented programming?
questions.option_a: Base classes compiled with older compilers crashing the JVM
questions.option_b: Seemingly safe modifications to a base class unintentionally breaking derived classes because derived classes depend on internal base implementation details
questions.option_c: Base classes that exceed 1000 lines of code
questions.option_d: A base class that has no default constructor
questions.explanation: Tight coupling between base and subclasses means changes to private workflows or method calling sequences in the base class can corrupt derived class invariants.

questions.question_text: What problem does the Visitor Design Pattern solve in object-oriented class hierarchies?
questions.option_a: It allows adding new operations to existing class structures without modifying the classes themselves, via double dispatch
questions.option_b: It converts binary trees into linked lists
questions.option_c: It automatically serializes objects to JSON
questions.option_d: It enables circular inheritance without compiler errors
questions.explanation: Visitor separates algorithms from the object structures on which they operate by using double dispatch (element.accept(visitor) calling visitor.visit(element)).

questions.question_text: Which design pattern defines a family of algorithms, encapsulates each one, and makes them interchangeable at runtime?
questions.option_b: Decorator Pattern
questions.explanation: The Strategy pattern decouples algorithm selection from client code, enabling clients to switch strategies dynamically without changing context.

questions.question_text: Which design pattern is used to attach additional responsibilities to an object dynamically without modifying the original class hierarchy?
questions.option_b: Composite Pattern
questions.explanation: The Decorator pattern wraps an object to dynamically extend its functionality at runtime as an alternative to subclassing.

questions.question_text: Why should a base class destructor always be declared virtual when polymorphism is used in C++?
questions.option_b: To ensure the derived class destructor is invoked when deleting a derived object through a base class pointer, preventing resource leaks
questions.option_c: To enable garbage collection in C++
questions.option_d: To allow constructors to be inherited
questions.explanation: Deleting an object of derived type through a pointer to base with a non-virtual destructor results in undefined behavior and resource leakage as the derived destructor is skipped.

questions.question_text: How is dynamic dispatch (runtime polymorphism) implemented under the hood in C++?
questions.option_b: Using Virtual Method Tables (vtable) and virtual table pointers (vptr) in each object
questions.option_c: Using if-else switch statements injected by the compiler
questions.option_d: Through dynamic memory allocation on every method call
questions.explanation: Each class with virtual functions has a static vtable of function pointers, and each object contains a vptr pointing to its class vtable.

questions.question_text: Liskov Substitution Principle?
questions.option_b: Subtypes substitutable for base
questions.explanation: LSP: subtypes must be substitutable

questions.question_text: The 'O' in SOLID design principles represents the Open-Closed Principle. What does it prescribe?
questions.option_a: Classes should be open for modification and closed for extension
questions.option_b: Software entities should be open for extension, but closed for modification
questions.option_c: Methods should only access public properties of their parameters
questions.option_d: Objects should only communicate with their immediate neighbors
questions.explanation: The Open-Closed Principle states that you should be able to extend class behavior without altering its existing source code.

questions.question_text: What does the 'S' in SOLID object-oriented design principles stand for?
questions.option_b: Single Responsibility Principle (a class should have one, and only one, reason to change)
questions.explanation: Single Responsibility Principle states that every module or class should have responsibility over a single part of the functionality and only one reason to change.

questions.question_text: What does the Dependency Inversion Principle (the 'D' in SOLID) mandate?
questions.option_a: High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both should depend on abstractions
questions.option_b: Classes must depend directly on concrete database drivers
questions.option_c: Inverting inheritance trees using multiple interfaces
questions.explanation: Dependency Inversion decouples high-level policy from low-level detail by introducing abstract interfaces between them.

questions.question_text: What does the Interface Segregation Principle (the 'I' in SOLID) recommend?
questions.option_a: All interfaces must inherit from a common root interface
questions.option_b: Clients should not be forced to depend upon interfaces that they do not use
questions.option_c: Every class must implement at least two interfaces
questions.option_d: Interfaces must contain only static constant fields
questions.explanation: Many client-specific fine-grained interfaces are better than one general-purpose interface to prevent implementing unused dummy methods.

questions.question_text: What does the Open/Closed Principle (the 'O' in SOLID) dictate?
questions.option_a: Classes should be open for modification, closed for extension
questions.option_b: Software entities should be open for extension, but closed for modification
questions.option_c: Methods should open all connections before execution and close them immediately
questions.explanation: Open/Closed Principle states that you should be able to extend a class's behavior without modifying its existing tested source code (e.g. via inheritance or composition).

questions.question_text: What is a Pure Virtual Function in C++?
questions.option_a: A virtual function declared with '= 0' that has no implementation in the base class and makes the class abstract
questions.option_b: A static function that cannot access members
questions.option_c: A function that has no side effects and returns const values
questions.option_d: A function defined in a separate DLL
questions.explanation: A pure virtual function (virtual void f() = 0;) forces derived classes to provide an override before they can be instantiated.

questions.question_text: What is the Diamond Problem in multiple inheritance and how does C++ resolve it?
questions.option_a: Stack overflow caused by recursive calls; resolved by tail call optimization
questions.option_b: Ambiguity when a class inherits from two classes that both inherit from a common base; resolved by virtual inheritance
questions.option_c: Memory leaks in circular references; resolved by shared_ptr
questions.option_d: Virtual table corruption; resolved by final keyword
questions.explanation: The diamond problem occurs when child D inherits from B and C, both inheriting from A; virtual inheritance (virtual public A) ensures only one shared instance of A exists.

questions.question_text: What is the difference between Composition and Aggregation in OOP object relationships?
questions.option_a: Composition represents 'Has-A' with strong ownership (child cannot exist without parent); Aggregation represents 'Has-A' with weak ownership (child can exist independently)
questions.option_b: Aggregation is inheritance; Composition is polymorphism
questions.option_c: Composition uses pointers; Aggregation uses values
questions.explanation: In Composition, the child's lifecycle is bound to the parent (e.g. Room in a House); in Aggregation, children can outlive the parent (e.g. Teacher in a School).

questions.question_text: What is the difference between shallow copy and deep copy?
questions.option_a: Shallow copy copies reference pointers; deep copy recursively duplicates the referenced objects and their memory
questions.option_b: Shallow copy creates two completely independent copies in memory
questions.option_c: Deep copy only copies primitive numbers
questions.explanation: A shallow copy copies field values directly, so reference fields point to the same shared memory; a deep copy duplicates referenced memory blocks.

questions.question_text: Which Creational Design Pattern ensures that only one instance of a class exists throughout application runtime?
questions.option_b: Singleton Pattern
questions.explanation: Singleton restricts the instantiation of a class to one single global instance and provides a global access point to it.

questions.question_text: Which behavioral design pattern defines a one-to-many dependency so that when one object changes state, all its dependents are notified automatically?
questions.option_b: Strategy Pattern
questions.explanation: Observer pattern decouples subject and observers, notifying all registered observers upon state change (publish-subscribe).

questions.question_text: Which pattern ensures single instance?
questions.option_b: Observer
questions.explanation: Singleton restricts to one object

questions.question_text: Which structural design pattern allows incompatible interfaces to work together by wrapping an existing class with a new interface?
questions.option_b: Adapter Pattern
questions.explanation: Adapter translates the interface of one existing class into another interface that clients expect.

questions.question_text: Virtual memory?
questions.option_b: Disk used as RAM extension
questions.explanation: Virtual memory extends RAM using disk

questions.question_text: What does PCB stand for in operating systems?
questions.option_b: Program Communication Bus
questions.explanation: The PCB (Process Control Block) stores context information (PID, state, program counter, registers, memory limits) for a process.

questions.question_text: What is Deadlock in operating systems?
questions.option_a: A situation where a set of processes are blocked because each is holding a resource and waiting for another held by another process
questions.option_b: A system shutdown due to power failure
questions.option_d: An infinite loop in user mode
questions.explanation: Deadlock occurs when processes form a circular wait for exclusive resources, preventing any from making progress.

questions.question_text: What is Spooling in operating systems?
questions.option_a: Simultaneous Peripheral Operations On-Line (putting jobs in a buffer/disk queue, e.g. print spooling)
questions.option_b: Stopping CPU clocks to save energy
questions.explanation: Spooling buffers I/O jobs on secondary storage so devices of different speeds (like printers) can process data asynchronously.

questions.question_text: What is a Page Fault in an operating system?
questions.option_a: A hardware failure of the RAM module
questions.option_b: An interrupt generated when a program attempts to access a page of memory mapped into virtual address space but not loaded in physical RAM
questions.explanation: A page fault triggers the OS page-fault handler to retrieve the required page from disk into a free RAM frame.

questions.question_text: What is a system call?
questions.option_a: A phone call to technical support
questions.option_b: The programmatic interface by which an application requests a service from the operating system kernel
questions.option_c: A hardware interrupt from the keyboard
questions.explanation: System calls (e.g. read, write, fork) switch CPU from user mode to kernel mode to perform privileged hardware operations.

questions.question_text: What is an interrupt in an operating system?
questions.option_b: A hardware or software signal alerting the CPU that an event requires immediate attention
questions.option_c: An infinite loop in user code
questions.explanation: An interrupt causes the CPU to save its current execution context and transfer control to an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR).

questions.question_text: What is context switching?
questions.option_b: Saving the state of the currently executing process/thread and restoring the state of another so execution can be resumed
questions.explanation: Context switching enables multitasking by saving register values and state of one process and loading another into the CPU.

questions.question_text: What is the key difference between a Process and a Thread?
questions.option_a: A process shares memory with other processes; threads have isolated address spaces
questions.option_b: A process is an executing program with its own address space; a thread is a lightweight execution path within a process sharing memory
questions.option_c: Threads are hardware devices; processes are software
questions.explanation: Processes are isolated execution environments with independent memory; threads within the same process share code, data, and heap.

questions.question_text: What is the primary function of the Operating System Kernel?
questions.option_b: Manage system hardware resources and provide core services to applications
questions.explanation: The kernel is the central component of an OS managing CPU scheduling, memory, hardware devices, and system calls.

questions.question_text: What is the primary role of the Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB)?
questions.option_a: Cache page table translations to speed up virtual memory access
questions.option_b: Buffer I/O disk sector requests
questions.option_c: Store CPU register context during interrupts
questions.explanation: The TLB is a high-speed hardware associative cache that stores recent virtual-to-physical address mappings.

questions.question_text: Which CPU scheduling algorithm allocates fixed time quantum slices to each process in cyclic order?
questions.option_b: Priority Scheduling
questions.explanation: Round Robin assigns a uniform time slice (quantum) to each ready process in circular FIFO order.

questions.question_text: Which CPU scheduling algorithm schedules processes in the order of their arrival?
questions.option_b: First-Come, First-Served (FCFS)
questions.explanation: FCFS assigns CPU time non-preemptively based strictly on the arrival sequence of processes in the ready queue.

questions.question_text: Which command is used to view running processes in Linux?
questions.option_b: ps (or top/htop)
questions.explanation: The ps command displays information about active system processes.

questions.question_text: Which memory management scheme allows the execution of processes that are not completely loaded into physical RAM?
questions.option_b: Virtual Memory (Paging)
questions.explanation: Virtual memory uses secondary storage (swap/paging) to simulate more RAM than physically exists, bringing pages on demand.

questions.question_text: Consider a system using Peterson's algorithm for mutual exclusion between two processes P0 and P1. Which shared variables are used?
questions.option_a: A binary semaphore and a counting semaphore
questions.option_b: An integer turn variable and a boolean flag array flag[2]
questions.option_c: A mutex lock and a condition variable
questions.explanation: Peterson's algorithm relies on 'int turn' and 'bool flag[2]' to ensure mutual exclusion, progress, and bounded waiting in software.

questions.question_text: How does Copy-On-Write (COW) optimize the 'fork()' system call in modern operating systems?
questions.option_a: It copies all memory pages into swap disk before forking
questions.option_b: Child and parent share the same physical memory pages marked read-only; a page is duplicated only when either process attempts to write to it
