questions.option_c: It executes child and parent sequentially
questions.option_d: It skips creating a new process control block
questions.explanation: COW avoids unnecessary page copying by sharing physical pages until one process performs a write, triggering a page-fault that allocates a private page replica.

questions.question_text: How does Memory Compaction address external fragmentation in variable-partition memory management?
questions.option_a: It compresses text files on disk
questions.option_b: It relocates active processes to one end of memory, consolidating all free space into one large contiguous block
questions.option_c: It converts physical memory into swap space
questions.explanation: Memory compaction shuffles allocated memory partitions contiguously at runtime (requiring dynamic address binding with base/limit registers) to aggregate free fragments.

questions.question_text: In Linux, what is the Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS) and what data structure does it use to select the next task?
questions.option_b: A Red-Black tree tracking virtual runtime (vruntime) of runnable tasks, picking the leftmost node with minimum vruntime
questions.explanation: CFS uses an augmented Red-Black tree ordered by vruntime to guarantee O(log N) scheduling decisions that approximate ideal multi-tasking hardware.

questions.question_text: In the context of the Banker's Algorithm for deadlock avoidance, a state is considered 'Safe' if:
questions.option_a: All resources are currently free and unallocated
questions.option_b: There exists at least one sequence of process execution that allows every process to complete without deadlock
questions.option_c: No process requests more than half of the total resource pool
questions.option_d: Every requested resource can be immediately allocated upon demand
questions.explanation: A safe state guarantees that a safe sequence <P1, P2, ... Pn> exists such that each process's maximum claims can be met with currently available + already allocated resources.

questions.question_text: What causes False Sharing in multi-threaded programs on multi-core SMP systems?
questions.option_a: Threads sharing the same global variable name
questions.option_b: Threads on different cores modifying independent variables that reside within the same CPU cache line (typically 64 bytes), triggering continuous cache coherency invalidations
questions.option_d: A compiler bug in loop unrolling
questions.explanation: Because cache coherency (e.g. MESI protocol) operates at cache-line granularity (64 bytes), updates to adjacent independent variables invalidate the whole line across cores.

questions.question_text: What does a Multi-Level Inverted Page Table do to reduce page table memory overhead in 64-bit systems?
questions.option_a: Indexes entries by physical frame numbers rather than virtual page numbers, using a hash anchor table
questions.option_b: Stores page tables on secondary flash drives
questions.option_c: Disables virtual memory translation for kernel threads
questions.explanation: Inverted page tables maintain one entry per physical frame rather than per virtual page, drastically reducing page table memory in large 64-bit address spaces.

questions.question_text: What hardware atomic instruction is primarily utilized to implement spinlocks and mutual exclusion primitives on modern multi-core x86/ARM processors?
questions.option_b: Compare-And-Swap (CAS) / Test-And-Set (or LL/SC on ARM)
questions.explanation: Atomic Read-Modify-Write instructions like CMPXCHG (x86) and Load-Linked/Store-Conditional (ARM) atomically test and update memory without interleaving.

questions.question_text: What is Priority Inversion and how is it resolved in real-time operating systems?
questions.option_a: High-priority process blocked waiting for a resource held by low-priority process, while medium-priority processes preempt the low-priority process; solved by Priority Inheritance Protocol
questions.option_b: Processes having negative nice values; solved by renice
questions.option_c: Round-robin schedulers ignoring priority; solved by FCFS
questions.option_d: Starvation of low-priority threads; solved by aging
questions.explanation: Mars Pathfinder bug: Priority Inheritance temporarily elevates the priority of the low-priority resource holder to that of the highest blocked waiting process.

questions.question_text: What is an Orphan Process in Unix/Linux and who adopts it?
questions.option_a: A process with no PID; adopted by the kernel idle task
questions.option_b: A child process whose parent terminated without waiting; adopted by the init process (systemd / PID 1)
questions.option_d: A thread detached from its process
questions.explanation: When a parent process exits before its children, the orphaned children are adopted by PID 1 (init/systemd), which periodically reaps their exit statuses.

questions.question_text: What is the ABA problem in lock-free concurrent programming using Compare-And-Swap (CAS)?
questions.option_a: A thread reads value A, is preempted, other threads change A -> B -> A, and the original thread CAS succeeds unaware that intermediate modifications occurred
questions.option_b: A deadlock between two mutexes
questions.explanation: CAS compares value equality, so if a memory location returns to A after intermediate changes (A -> B -> A), CAS incorrectly assumes nothing changed (often leading to use-after-free in lock-free stacks).

questions.question_text: What is the difference between Hard Real-Time and Soft Real-Time operating systems?
questions.option_a: Hard real-time guarantees that meeting deadlines is mandatory and missing a deadline results in total system failure; soft real-time degrades quality of service if deadlines are missed
questions.option_b: Hard real-time runs only on microcontrollers
questions.option_c: Soft real-time uses no priority scheduling
questions.option_d: Hard real-time does not support interrupts
questions.explanation: In hard real-time systems (e.g. avionics, pacemaker), missing a strict deadline causes catastrophic failure; soft real-time (e.g. video streaming) tolerates occasional latencies.

questions.question_text: What is the difference between Peterson's Algorithm and Lamport's Bakery Algorithm?
questions.option_a: Peterson's algorithm is restricted to 2 processes; Lamport's Bakery algorithm provides mutual exclusion for N concurrent processes
questions.option_b: Peterson's requires hardware support; Bakery is software only
questions.option_c: Bakery algorithm works only on single-core CPUs
questions.option_d: Peterson's algorithm cannot avoid race conditions
questions.explanation: Peterson's algorithm solves mutual exclusion for exactly two processes using flag and turn variables; Lamport's Bakery algorithm generalizes to N processes using ticket numbers.

questions.question_text: What is the difference between monolithic kernels and microkernels?
questions.option_a: Monolithic kernels run all core OS services (FS, drivers, IPC, networking) in kernel space; microkernels keep only minimal mechanisms (IPC, low-level scheduling) in kernel space and run services in user space
questions.option_b: Monolithic kernels are written in assembly; microkernels in C
questions.option_c: Microkernels are always faster than monolithic kernels
questions.explanation: Monolithic kernels provide high performance via direct in-kernel function calls; microkernels offer fault isolation and modularity by running drivers and filesystems as user-space daemons.

questions.question_text: What is the purpose of the OOM (Out Of Memory) Killer in the Linux kernel?
questions.option_a: To alert the user via desktop notification
questions.option_b: When physical RAM and swap are completely exhausted, it calculates badness heuristics to select and sacrifice a process (SIGKILL) to prevent total kernel panic
questions.option_c: To dynamically compress inactive memory pages
questions.option_d: To increase swap partition size automatically
questions.explanation: The Linux OOM killer scores processes based on RSS, oom_score_adj, and privilege, terminating the highest scoring process to restore system stability.

questions.question_text: Semaphore used for?
questions.option_b: Process sync
questions.explanation: Semaphores control shared resource access

questions.question_text: What are the four Coffman conditions required for a deadlock to occur?
questions.option_a: Mutual Exclusion, Hold and Wait, No Preemption, Circular Wait
questions.option_b: Preemption, Starvation, Paging, Fragmentation
questions.explanation: All four conditions (Mutual exclusion, Hold & wait, No preemption, Circular wait) must hold simultaneously for a deadlock to exist.

questions.question_text: What does the 'fork()' system call do in Unix/Linux?
questions.option_a: Creates a new thread in the same process
questions.option_b: Creates a new child process that is an exact duplicate of the calling parent process with its own unique PID
questions.explanation: fork() spawns an identical child process; fork() returns 0 to the child and the child's PID to the parent.

questions.question_text: What is Belady's Anomaly in page replacement algorithms?
questions.option_a: LRU algorithm page fault count increasing with more page frames
questions.option_b: FIFO page replacement experiencing MORE page faults when physical memory frames are INCREASED
questions.explanation: Belady's Anomaly shows that for certain reference strings under FIFO page replacement, allocating more physical frames actually increases total page faults.

questions.question_text: What is Thrashing in virtual memory systems?
questions.option_a: When CPU runs at 100% processing user computations
questions.option_b: When the operating system spends more time servicing page faults and swapping pages than executing instructions
questions.option_c: When hard disks spin too fast
questions.option_d: When cache memory is completely disabled
questions.explanation: Thrashing happens when the sum of processes' working sets exceeds available physical frames, causing continuous disk paging.

questions.question_text: What is a Counting Semaphore vs a Binary Semaphore (Mutex)?
questions.option_a: A binary semaphore has values 0 and 1; a counting semaphore has an integer range used to control access to a finite pool of resources
questions.option_b: A counting semaphore cannot block processes
questions.option_c: A mutex can be accessed by any number of processes simultaneously
questions.option_d: A binary semaphore runs only on dual-core CPUs
questions.explanation: Binary semaphores act as mutual exclusion locks (0/1); counting semaphores maintain a counter initialized to N available resource instances.

questions.question_text: What is a Zombie Process in Unix/Linux?
questions.option_a: A process that consumes 100% CPU in an infinite loop
questions.option_b: A process that has completed execution but still has an entry in the process table because its parent has not yet read its exit status with wait()
questions.option_d: A process running without a GUI
questions.explanation: A zombie process has released its memory but retains its PCB entry until the parent acknowledges its exit status via wait()/waitpid().

questions.question_text: What is the Banker's Algorithm used for in operating systems?
questions.option_b: Deadlock avoidance (by testing safety state before allocating resources)
questions.explanation: Dijkstra's Banker's Algorithm tests whether allocating resources to a requesting process leaves the system in a safe state.

questions.question_text: What is the Dining Philosophers Problem used to illustrate in computer science?
questions.option_b: Synchronization problems, deadlock, and starvation when concurrent processes share limited resources
questions.explanation: Dijkstra's Dining Philosophers problem models resource contention and circular waiting where processes require multiple simultaneous shared locks.

questions.question_text: What is the Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB)?
questions.option_b: A high-speed hardware associative cache that stores recent virtual-to-physical address page translations
questions.option_c: A table storing hard disk sector maps
questions.option_d: A register holding the program counter
questions.explanation: The TLB caches page table entries in hardware near the MMU, speeding up virtual address translation from memory lookups to single-cycle cache lookups.

questions.question_text: What is the difference between Internal and External Fragmentation?
questions.option_a: Internal is wasted space within an allocated block/page; External is unallocated memory between allocated blocks too small to satisfy requests
questions.option_b: Internal occurs on disk; External occurs in RAM
questions.option_c: Internal can be solved by compaction; External cannot
questions.explanation: Internal fragmentation occurs when allocated units are larger than requested; external fragmentation occurs when free memory is divided into unusable scattered holes.

questions.question_text: What is the difference between Preemptive and Non-Preemptive CPU scheduling?
questions.option_a: Preemptive can interrupt a running process before its CPU burst finishes; Non-preemptive lets a process run until it voluntarily yields or blocks
questions.option_b: Preemptive applies only to real-time systems
questions.option_d: Preemptive scheduling requires no timer hardware
questions.explanation: Preemptive schedulers use hardware clock interrupts to forcibly context-switch running processes to enforce fairness.

questions.question_text: What phenomenon occurs when excessive page faults lead to continuous paging activity, causing CPU utilization to drop dramatically?
questions.option_b: Thrashing
questions.explanation: Thrashing occurs when the total working sets of active processes exceed available physical memory, spending more time swapping than executing.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT one of the four Coffman conditions necessary for a deadlock to occur?
questions.option_b: Hold and Wait
questions.explanation: The condition is 'No Preemption'. If preemption is allowed, deadlock cannot persist because resources can be reclaimed.

questions.question_text: Which page replacement algorithm is immune to Belady's Anomaly because it belongs to the class of 'Stack Algorithms'?
questions.option_b: LRU (Least Recently Used)
questions.explanation: Stack algorithms (like LRU and Optimal) guarantee that the set of pages in memory for N frames is always a subset of pages in memory for N+1 frames.
